newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian police use water cannon to end protest.
newsitem.headline: Serbian police use water cannon to end protest.

text.p: Serbia anti-riot police using water cannon, batons and shields forcibly cleared demonstrators from a river bridge in central Belgrade on Sunday after an angry stand-off, witnesses said.

It was the first time that water cannon had been used in 77 days of street protests demanding that the hitherto monolithic socialist government of President Slobodan Milosevic must recognise opposition victories in local elections last November.

Witnesses said they saw police using their shields to forcibly push demonstrators away. Some protesters burned tyres, hurled bottles at police lines and threw concrete blocks into the road, apparently to impede the water cannon trucks.
"They (police) also used their batons to hit people," said one cameraman. "They moved fast and the protesters fell back."
Demonstrators, some of them drenched by the water cannon screamed "traitors" and "fascists" at the police.
Blood poured down the face of one man and other people were also hurt, witnesses said, but details were sketchy.

The police moved in just before midnight at both ends of the bridge after opposition politicians urged their supporters to stay in place all night if necessary, effectively laying siege to the police.
Tens of thousands of opposition supporters had converged on the Brankov bridge, which links old and new quarters of the Serbian capital, on a bend in the Sava River.
The stand-off began after a police cordon established on the bridge halted a relatively small contingent of several hundred protesters heading towards the city centre.
Other, larger groups of demonstrators heard the news and quickly changed course for the bridge, so that both ends of the concrete structure were blocked off.
It was not clear why the police took up positions on the bridge in the first place, leaving avenues in the old city wide open.
But their move acted like a magnet on the marchers who have gathered every day in a central square to hear pro-democracy speeches by their leaders.
Under the relentless pressure of the daily protests, fissures have began opening up within Milosevic'sa increasingly weak and isolated socialist establishment.
More than 1,000 shools are shut, teachers are on strike, universities are in turmoil, lawyers are rallying with student protesters and the ruling socialists seem divided.
The junior New Democracy party in Milosevic's leftist coalition, echoing churchmen and senior soldiers, has openly called for the opposition election wins to be reinstated.
